title: Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE)
summary: Describes Interactive Connectivity Establishment, a way to get through NATs for UDP media sessions set up with the offer/answer model. It uses STUN and TURN to try several routes and choose a working one, and it can be used with protocols like SIP. It was replaced by RFC 8445 and RFC 8839. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary:
A NAT sits between your computer and the internet and hides the address your computer actually has. ICE solves the problem by making both sides try every possible route and keeping the one that works.

The routes are listed in the call setup, so both sides learn each other's options before any media flows, and a short test message proves which route is real.

questions: how does nat traversal work for voip
how does ice nat traversal work
what is the difference between host and relayed candidates
subtitle: How two endpoints behind NATs gather, test and choose a working network path for a UDP media session.

tldr.problem: Two computers that want to send voice or video to each other usually sit behind NATs, and neither knows the address the other can reach. Every existing trick for getting through a NAT works in some networks and not others.
tldr.mechanism: ICE collects every address each side might have, puts them in the call setup, then tries the combinations one by one with a short STUN exchange until a working one is found. The pair that works becomes the path for the media.
tldr.outcome: The RFC became a Proposed Standard and was later replaced by RFC 8445 and RFC 8839. It also deprecated RFC 4091 and RFC 4092, and the IAB called it a short-term mechanism with its own exit strategy.

today: RFC 5245 was a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 8445, which revises the ICE protocol itself, and RFC 8839, which covers the offer and answer procedures for ICE. The document itself treats ICE as a short-term mechanism with an exit strategy.

sections.title: Why ICE Exists
sections.content:
There are many techniques for getting media through a NAT, and each one has advantages and disadvantages that make it optimal in some network topologies and a poor choice in others. The result is that administrators and implementors end up making assumptions about the topologies of the networks in which their solutions will be deployed, which introduces complexity and brittleness. What is needed is a single solution flexible enough to work well in all situations.

This specification defines Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) as a technique for NAT traversal for UDP-based media streams established with the offer/answer model, although ICE can be extended to handle other transport protocols such as TCP. ICE is an extension to the offer/answer model and works by including a multiplicity of IP addresses and ports in the SDP offer and answer, which are then tested for connectivity by peer-to-peer connectivity checks.

The addresses and the checks use the revised STUN specification, now named Session Traversal Utilities for NAT, whose new name reflects its new role as a tool used with other NAT traversal techniques rather than a standalone solution. ICE also makes use of TURN, an extension to STUN. Because ICE exchanges a multiplicity of IP addresses and ports for each media stream, it also allows for address selection for multihomed and dual-stack hosts, and for this reason it deprecates RFC 4091 and RFC 4092.

In a typical deployment there are two endpoints, known as agents in the offer/answer terminology, that want to communicate. They communicate indirectly through a signalling protocol such as SIP, which carries the offer and answer exchange of SDP messages. At the beginning of the ICE process the agents are ignorant of their own topologies: they might or might not be behind a NAT, or behind several NATs in series. ICE allows the agents to discover enough information about their topologies to find one or more paths by which they can communicate.
sections.plainLanguage: ICE replaces a pile of special cases with one procedure that works the same way everywhere. The cost is a few extra round trips while the two sides work out which path to use.

sections.title: Candidates: the Addresses ICE Tries
sections.content:
Each agent has a variety of candidate transport addresses it could use to reach the other agent. A transport address is a combination of IP address and port for a particular transport protocol, which is always UDP in this specification. A candidate is such a transport address, and the document defines three types that are gathered, plus one that is learned during the checks.

A host candidate is a transport address obtained directly from a local interface. The interface could be Ethernet or Wi-Fi, or one obtained through a tunnel mechanism such as a VPN or Mobile IP. If the agent is multihomed it obtains a candidate from each IP address, and rather than guessing which one the peer can reach, the offering agent includes them all in its offer.

The agent then uses STUN or TURN to obtain two more kinds. A server reflexive candidate is a translated address on the public side of a NAT. A relayed candidate is an address allocated by a TURN server, which acts as a packet relay forwarding traffic between the two agents. When TURN servers are used, both kinds are obtained from the TURN server. The host candidate associated with a given server reflexive candidate is called its base, the address the agent sends from for that candidate. If the agent is not behind a NAT the base is the same as the server reflexive candidate, and the server reflexive candidate is redundant and is eliminated.

A peer reflexive candidate is not gathered at all. Because the connectivity check is a STUN Binding request, the response carries the sender's translated transport address on the public side of any NAT between the agent and its peer. If that address differs from the candidates already learned, it is a new candidate, and ICE tests it exactly like any other.
sections.plainLanguage: Each address a side might use is called a candidate. Some come from the machine itself, some from the NAT in front of it, and some from a relay server. A fourth kind turns up by accident during the tests and is used too.

sections.title: Connectivity Checks
sections.content:
Once L has gathered all of its candidates, it orders them from highest to lowest priority and sends them to R over the signalling channel, carried in attributes in the SDP offer. When R receives the offer it performs the same gathering process and responds with its own list. At the end of this each agent has a complete list of both its candidates and its peer's candidates, and pairs them up into candidate pairs.

To see which pairs work, each agent schedules a series of checks. Each check is a STUN request and response transaction, performed on one candidate pair by sending a STUN request from the local candidate to the remote candidate. The principle is simple: sort the candidate pairs in priority order, send checks on each pair in that order, and acknowledge the checks received from the other agent.

With both agents performing a check on a pair, the result is a four-way handshake: L sends a STUN request to R, R answers with a STUN response, R sends a STUN request back to L, and L answers with a STUN response. At the end of it both sides know that they can send and receive messages end to end in both directions. As an optimisation, as soon as R gets L's check it schedules a check back to L on the same pair; this is called a triggered check, and it speeds up the discovery of a valid candidate.

The STUN requests are sent to and from the exact same IP addresses and ports that will be used for media such as RTP and RTCP. The agents therefore demultiplex STUN from RTP and RTCP using the contents of the packets rather than the port on which they arrive.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides test the same pair at the same time, which takes four short messages. When all four arrive, each side knows the other can hear it.

sections.title: Sorting Candidates and Choosing a Pair
sections.content:
Because the algorithm searches all candidate pairs, if a working pair exists it will eventually find it whatever order the candidates are tried in. To produce faster and better results the candidates are sorted in a specified order, and the resulting list of sorted candidate pairs is called the check list. Two general principles apply. Each agent gives its candidates a numeric priority, which is sent along with the candidate to the peer. The local and remote priorities are combined so that each agent has the same ordering for the candidate pairs, which matters when NATs are in front of both ends, because NATs often refuse packets from a host until that host has sent a packet towards it first.

The priority formula combines a preference for each type of candidate and, when the agent is multihomed, a preference for its IP addresses: priority = (2^24)*(type preference) + (2^8)*(local preference) + (2^0)*(256 - component ID). The type preference is an integer from 0 to 126 and must be the same for all candidates of one type and different for different types, with the preference for peer reflexive candidates higher than for server reflexive ones. The local preference is an integer from 0 to 65535, and the component ID must be between 1 and 256.

Candidates of similar type are given similar priorities, and more direct routes, through fewer relays and fewer NATs, are preferred over indirect ones. To avoid testing the same kind of route again and again, each candidate carries a foundation, and two candidates share one when they are of the same type and came from the same host candidate and STUN server using the same protocol. Initially only the pairs with unique foundations are tested and the rest are marked frozen; when a check succeeds the other pairs with that foundation are unfrozen.

To conclude, ICE assigns one agent the role of controlling agent and the other the role of controlled agent. The controlling agent nominates which of the valid pairs will carry the media. With regular nomination it lets the checks continue until at least one valid pair is found for each media stream, then picks among the valid ones and sends a second STUN request on its nominated pair with a flag telling the peer that the pair has been nominated. With aggressive nomination it puts the flag in every STUN request, so the first successful check ends the processing for that media stream and no second request is needed. Aggressive nomination is faster but gives less flexibility. The pair actually used for media is called the selected pair.
sections.plainLanguage: The candidates are ranked so that the most direct routes are tried first, and one side is given the final say about which of the working routes to use.

sections.title: Full and Lite Implementations
sections.content:
Both agents need to support ICE for a call to use it. However, certain agents are always connected to the public Internet and have a public IP address at which they can receive packets from any correspondent. To make it easier for these devices to support ICE, the RFC defines a special type of implementation called lite, in contrast to the normal full implementation.

A lite implementation does not gather candidates; it includes only host candidates for any media stream. Lite agents do not generate connectivity checks or run the state machines, though they must be able to respond to connectivity checks. When a lite implementation connects with a full implementation, the full agent takes the role of controlling agent and the lite agent takes the controlled role. When two lite implementations connect, no checks are sent at all. The RFC notes that the lite implementation was added as a stepping stone to full implementation, and that a full implementation is preferable if it can be achieved.

The IAB's section of the RFC treats ICE as a short-term mechanism that must justify itself. It records the two specific problems ICE solves: giving two peers a way to determine the set of transport addresses that can be used for communication, and giving an agent a way to determine an address that is reachable by another peer. On the exit strategy, the IAB observes that ICE does not easily get phased out, but that it helps phase out other short-term mechanisms by selecting among them and preferring the better ones. As NATs dissipate with IPv6, server reflexive and relayed candidates simply never get used, because higher-priority connectivity exists to the native host candidates, so the servers are used less and less. On brittleness, the IAB concludes that ICE removes brittleness from classic STUN rather than adding it, since it drops the error-prone process of classifying the NAT type and lets the agents connect directly when they can, with the penalty that session establishment takes longer.
sections.plainLanguage: A device with a public address can skip most of the work, and the IAB's view is that ICE is a stopgap that will matter less as IPv6 replaces NATs.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because ICE is used to discover which addresses can be used to send media between two agents, it matters that the process cannot be hijacked to send media to the wrong location. Each STUN connectivity check is covered by a message authentication code computed with a key exchanged in the signalling channel. This gives message integrity and data origin authentication, so an attacker cannot forge or modify connectivity check messages. When a SIP call forks, the ICE exchanges happen independently with each forked recipient, and the keys exchanged in the signalling help associate each exchange with each recipient.

The RFC lists the false conclusions an attacker might try to force: that a candidate pair is invalid when it is not, that it is valid when it is not, that a peer reflexive candidate exists when it should not, and that a candidate the attacker invented is valid. Most of these are prevented by the STUN short-term credential mechanism, because the attacker has to inject a fake response that must be processed and needs the password to do so, and by securing the offer and answer exchange. Forcing a false invalid result also needs the real response to be dropped, and if it is not dropped the success response alerts the originator to a possible attack.

The remaining attack, using packet replays to force a false peer reflexive candidate, is hard to launch because it requires the attacker to intercept and replay packets sent by two different hosts at the same time. If SRTP is used the attacker cannot play the media packets but can discard them, disabling the media stream for the call, although disrupting the media directly would be easier than attacking ICE. The RFC also lists attacks on server reflexive address gathering, on relayed candidate gathering and on the offer and answer exchanges, and two insider attacks, the voice hammer attack and the STUN amplification attack. Among the countermeasures it recommends using ICE with secure signalling techniques such as SIPS, and limiting the total number of connectivity checks to 100.
sections.plainLanguage: Every test message is signed with a key that only the two ends know, so a stranger cannot make a fake test look real. The RFC also says to cap the number of tests an offer can cause, so that a malicious caller cannot turn ICE into a way to attack the network.

viz.caption: The four kinds of ICE candidate

items.title: Host candidate
items.text: A transport address taken straight from a local interface, such as Ethernet, Wi-Fi, a VPN or Mobile IP.

items.title: Server reflexive candidate
items.text: The translated address on the public side of a NAT, learned from a STUN server or from the TURN server.

items.title: Relayed candidate
items.text: An address allocated by a TURN server, which then relays the media between the two agents.

items.title: Peer reflexive candidate
items.text: A new address discovered from the STUN response of a connectivity check, and tested like any other candidate.
